title_original: Deadline’s Reviews Of This Thanksgiving’s Box Office Openers: ‘Hexed’, ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ & ‘Focker-In-Law’
excerpt_original: This week’s theatrical releases continue the march into movie awards season, with the emergence on U.S. screens of animation, comedy and action that have been long-awaited in this final stretch of the year. Deadline has compiled its list of movies we’ve reviewed across the year…

blocks.text: This week’s theatrical releases continue the march into movie awards season, with the emergence on U.S. screens of films that started their journeys with buzzy festival launches as far back as Sundance.
Deadline has compiled its list of movies we’ve reviewed across the year that are now hitting cinemas.
RELATED: 53 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026

links.text: 53 Of The Most Anticipated Movies Of 2026

blocks.text: This week’s major new wide release is the return to Panem with the prequel The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping , which is raking in box office for Lionsgate. Also punching its way to wide-release status is I Play Rocky , the Amazon MGM Studios pic from Peter Farrelly about the making of Sly Stallone’s iconic 1976 boxing pic. It has been gaining steam in limited release.

links.text: raking in box office
I Play Rocky ,

blocks.text: Among limited bows this frame come Elsinore , for which star Andrew Scott is getting awards-season heat; Josephine , the wrenching Sundance double-winner starring Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan; and Minotaur , the political drama from exiled Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev that won the Grand Prix at Cannes and is France’s submission to the 2027 International Feature Oscar race .

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Image Credit: Lionsgate Release: Wide Distributor: Lionsgate Director : Francis Lawrence Screenwriter: Billy Ray Cast: Joseph Zada, Whitney Peak, McKenna Grace, Ben Wang, Elle Fanning, Glenn Close, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Percy Daggs IV, Maya Hawke, Lili Taylor, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Molly McCann, Iona Bell, Kieran Culkin, Billy Porter Original review date: November 17, 2026 Deadline’s takeaway: Playing Haymitch as nothing at all like the adult Woody Harrelson he will later grow up into, Joseph Zada has a naïve, doe-eyed charm that helps suspend disbelief for at least two hours of the film’s increasingly tedious running time. There is no sense of peril at all in this installment, even when Snow finally gets round to getting his drawn-out revenge: The Hunger Games has reached its High School Musical moment where everyone gets a participation prize, and any significant death is obviously just an unfortunate accident. The cast of the original film appear briefly at the end; one can’t shake the feeling that it’s to pay their last respects. – DW RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Review: Is Time Finally Running Out For The Dystopic Game Show Franchise?

blocks.text: ‘Elsinore’ Image Credit: Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC Release: Limited Distributor: Focus Features Director: Simon Stone Screenwriter: Stephen Beresford Cast: Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, Peter Mullen, Juliet Stevenson, Matthew Beard, David Dawson, Joe Locke, Luke Thomson Original review date: September 4, 2026 (Telluride Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: In the end though it is Scott triumphing here in a film that should make you sad but smartly doesn’t dwell on death, only life as we live it. It is the role of a lifetime playing someone getting the chance to play their role of a lifetime, which is saying a lot since Scott was equally brilliant earlier this year as another real-life person, a reluctant WWII hero, in Pressure. Here he has given Ian Charleson a gift: another moment in the spotlight at the National, this time to share it with the entire world. I would recommend bringing along a value-sized box of tissues. You might need them all. – PH RELATED: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘Josephine’ Image Credit: Sumerian Pictures / Everett Collection Release: Limited Distributor: Sumerian Films Director-screenwriter: Beth de Araújo Cast: Mason Reeves, Channing Tatum, Gemma Chan, Philip Ettinger, Syra McCarthy, Eleanore Pienta Original review date: January 23, 2026 (Sundance Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: I am not sure there is an audience that is going to run to see this downbeat film, but it effectively offers a different POV on the human cost of rape and the frustration in the legal system. That part is personified by the female defense lawyer looking for any way to cast doubt on the victims in this case — one of them who, by association and as collateral damage, happens to be an 8-year-old child scarred for life by a quirk of fate. One can only hope that writer-director Beth de Araújo, in mirroring a harrowing event from her own childhood, finds a meaningful reception to her film and some comfort in knowing it might help others just like her. — PH RELATED: ‘Josephine’ Review: Channing Tatum & Gemma Chan In Earnest Drama Focused On Rape Through 8-Year-Old Child’s Eyes

blocks.text: ‘Minotaur’ Image Credit: Mubi Release: Limited Distributor: Mubi Director: Andrey Zvyagintsev Screenwriters: Simon Lyashenko, Andrey Zvyagintsev, Claude Chabrol Cast: Iris Lebedeva, Dmitriy Mazurov, Varvara Shmykova, Juris Žagars Original review date: May 19, 2026 (Cannes Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur is is actually based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife , the French film released in 1969, but in its details, atmosphere and moral force it is unmistakably Russian. The chronicle of crime and — for the rich, the influential and the crafty – the conspicuous absence of any punishment doesn’t quite match Zvyagintsev’s masterpiece Leviathan ‘s moral sweep or exquisite skewering of a system that ensures that crime pays. But it is a great piece of work and offers a masterclass in directorial discipline. — SB RELATED: ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Ambiguous Thriller Exquisitely Skewers Russian Corruption

blocks.text: ‘How To Rob A Bank’ Image Credit: Megan Schoenbachler Release: Wide Distributor: Amazon MGM Studios Director: David Leitch Screenwriter: Mark Bianculli Cast: Nicholas Hoult, John C. Reilly, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson Original review date: November 11, 2026 Deadline’s Takeaway: “Though often hectic and loud with the visuals as well as the noise, How to Rob a Bank suddenly becomes very basic in the final stretch, ditching all the digital for an analog ending that’s literally binary, in which the law faces down the villain and sees his younger self staring back (or is it the other way round?). Reilly just about pulls off his part of the deal — because, hey, he’s John C. Reilly, and character work is his thing — but Hoult (who would make a good Joker, by the way), doesn’t quite have the same luxury in weaving together the various elements, private and public, of his persona. In the same way, the film self-deconstructs itself so often it’s hard to get a grip on what it’s ultimately trying to say. But whenever it’s doing exactly what it says on the tin, it’s a blast.” – Damon Wise RELATED: ‘How To Rob A Bank’ Review: Crony Capitalism Gets Blowback In David Leitch’s Anarchic Heist Tutorial

He also realizes having a stake in these very recognizable characters is key to all of it working as well as it does, and casting actors on the level of Driver, Johansson and Teller makes this soar. In fact, this is some of the finest screen work for all three.” – PH RELATED: ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver, Miles Teller & Scarlett Johansson Find The Dark Side Of The American Dream In James Gray’s Riveting Crime Drama- Cannes Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘Club Kid’ Release: Limited Distributor: A24 Director/screenwriter: Jordan Firstman Cast: Jordan Firstman, Cara Delvingne, Reggie Absolom, Kirby Howell-Baptiste, Colleen Camp Original review date: Date (Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: “It’s a difficult not to think of Adam Sandler in the wretched Big Daddy , but though it does mine a very rich seam of sentiment, Club Kid never settles for such schmaltz. Although the father-child relationship is very much the focus, Firstman uses the setup to explore other issues, notably the pressures of being a single gay man trying to extricate himself from such a transient environment. Its anything-goes approach to sexuality is intoxicatingly inclusive, and despite the loucheness of the denizens of the demi-monde, the film will strike a chord with any retired party animal who, as David Bowie once put it, suddenly realizes they don’t want to go out any more — they just want to stay home and get things done.” – DW RELATED: ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Poignant Father-Son Comedy Is A Crowd-Pleaser With An Edge – Cannes Film Festival

blocks.text: ‘I Play Rocky’ Image Credit: Amazon MGM Release: Limited Distributor: Amazon MGM Studios Director: Peter Farrelly Screenwriter: Peter Gamble Cast: Anthony Ippolito, AnnaSophia Robb, Toby Kebbell, P.J. Byrne, Jay Duplass, Matt Dillon, Stephan James, Tracy Letts, Kiki Seto Original review date: September 12 (Toronto Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: In a year that marks the 50th anniversary of Rocky, a film that spawned five sequels and three more films in the Creed spinoff series with Michael B. Jordan, I Play Rocky brings us full circle right back to the beginning and manages to slyly recapture the fresh spirit that birthed it. This film has turned the making of Rocky into its own Rocky-like moment of triumph. blocks.text: ‘Jimmy’ Release: Wide Distributor: Fathom Entertainment Director: Aaron Burns Screenwriter: Justin Strawhand Cast: KJ Apa, Max Casella, Jen Lilley, Kara Killmer, Sarah Drew, Rob Riggle, Christopher McDonald, Neal McDonough, Jason Alexander, Julian Works Original review date: November 2, 2026 Deadline’s takeaway: “ Jimmy aims to change all that and bring this largely unpublicized part of Stewart’s life to the frontlines and give it the attention it deserves. The movie doesn’t ignore completely his status as a movie star or his film career, but that is just a starting-off point. That aspect comes more fully into view at the end of the war with his doubts, even depression, about his ability to return in front of the cameras after director Frank Capra (who previously directed Stewart in You Can’t Take It With You and Mr. Smith Goes To Washington )worked hard to convince the star to do a script he had, It’s a Wonderful Life. The film is far more effective when focusing on his experiences in the war and post-war dealing with what is now known as PTSD. When he’s trying to find his way and worth back into society — and Hollywood — Jimmy proves a cut above your average movie-star biopic.” – PH RELATED: ‘Jimmy’ Review: KJ Apa Expertly Channels James Stewart In An Inspiring Movie That Tells The Story The Beloved Oscar Winning Star Kept To Himself

blocks.text: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Release: Wide Distributor: Searchlight Director’screenwriter: Cast: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas, Tom Waits, Parker Posey Original review date: September 3 (Venice Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: “Ultimately this is a film about two guys, two friends who have spent their lives in the service of some, to be kind, questionable pursuits in the world of foreign policy, a job that has asked them to do things that can be horrifying in a profession that lives on the edge of darkness too much of the time. It takes a toll, but Chris and Lee are the same kind of lone gunslinger who have seen and done bad things, but with each other find a rare emotional connection and friendship that ties them together. Malkovich is the perfect if unexpected casting here and it is one of those performances that after you see it is hard to imagine another actor doing as well. Rockwell may not have quite the quotable off-the-wall dialogue McDonagh has gifted Malkovich but nevertheless anchors the relationship in such ways that really makes this story work as well as it does.” – PH RELATED: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: John Malkovich And Sam Rockwell Superb In Martin McDonagh’s Funny And Profound Film – Venice Film Festival

‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’ Image Credit: MRC Release: Wide (October 30) Distributor: Sony Pictures Classics Director-screenwriter: Noah Segan Cast: John Turturro, Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Will Price, Tatiana Maslany Original review date: January 27 (Sundance Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: John Turturro’s Harry is a throwback, and so is this movie, a modest but really rather mesmerizing and forlorn film, one that’s curated just as much as it is directed. It’s about things past, about things gone, but also things that won’t stay dead as much as society wants that to happen. It’s also a film about vanishing bohemia, and it’s no coincidence many of the film’s storied leads are played by leading lights of New York’s iconic indie movie scene. — DW RELATED: ‘The Only Living Pickpocket In New York’ Review: John Turturro Steals The Show In Noah Segan’s Mesmerizing Debut – Sundance Film Festival

Grant, Marli Siu, Nabhaan Rizwan, Gustav Lindh, Ella Bruccoleri, Ben Ashenden, Kiell Smith Binoe Original review date: October 22 Deadline’s takeaway: A hit at Sundance where it was picked up by Black Bear , this wry film from writer-directors Alex Huston and Eleanor Wilson is sexy and satirically funny, but also oddly haunting as a truly twisted fable that says its never too late to become your own best version of Cinderella. — PH RELATED: ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgård Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight

blocks.text: ‘Possible Love’ Image Credit: Joo Jae-bum/Netflix Release: Limited (October 23) Distributor: Netflix Director: Lee Chang-dong Screenwriters: Lee Chang-dong and Oh Jung-Mi Cast: Jeon Do-Yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-Jeung Original review date: September 6 (Venice Film Festival) Deadline’s takeaway: In some ways Lee Chang-dong‘s first film in eight years, which is South Korea’s official entry into the International Feature Film Oscar race , might remind you of the class divide in Bong Joon Ho’s Oscar-winning Parasite . But with a pandemic between that release and this one, Lee’s film carries a poignant subtext: a certain desire for love and longing in a world more split apart than ever, and one which for many seems like it all is out of reach. — PH RELATED: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Lee Chang -dong’s South Korean International Oscar Entry Is Powerful Story Of Class And Desire – Venice Film Festival
